fatal_errors: The proposed larger-particle, higher-power APS intervention conflicts with the demonstrated intervention: optimized low-temperature ID-HVAF deposition using fine 5–30 μm feedstock.
It does not specify a single intervention, instead combining particle-size change with increased power and alternatively suggesting preheating.
Increasing APS power to melt 45–90 μm particles may increase oxidation and does not establish that deposition efficiency or attainable thickness will improve.
No prior evidence is cited to support the proposed particle-size mechanism or outcome.
Relevant service boundaries—50 h isothermal oxidation at 1000–1150 °C and the longer-duration substrate-melting limitation—are absent.
explanation: The response recognizes the need to increase thickness while preserving integrity and limiting oxidation, and it proposes measurable comparisons with a nominal 15–45 μm baseline. However, it fails to reconstruct the optimized ID-HVAF route that produced an approximately 150 μm, 0.2%-porosity coating with 79% deposition efficiency and minimal as-sprayed oxidation. Its APS mechanism is only speculative: larger particles can have greater momentum and lower specific surface area, but they are also harder to melt, and raising plasma power can increase oxidation, phase alteration, residual stress, and substrate heating. The experiment has a clear general failure rule, but changing both particle size and torch power confounds attribution; a factorial design would be needed to discriminate their effects. It also omits phase retention, deposition efficiency, high-temperature alumina-TGO behavior, and explicit service-temperature/time tests. With no supporting evidence and substantial unresolved technical risks, this is an unsupported alternative rather than a plausible or partial reconstruction.
